subChunks.title: Advanced Dark Mode
subChunks.hookHtml: The Junior tier covered toggling .dark on html. This lesson covers the complete professional dark mode system: respecting the OS system preference, providing a user override, persisting the preference, multi-theme support, and building a token system that makes dark mode a variable swap rather than a class audit.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator: "Dark mode is not just inverting colours. A professional implementation respects the OS preference by default, survives a page reload, lets the user override their OS preference, and makes adding a third theme trivial. All of that with no duplicated components."

System preference + user override pattern

/* index.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));

/* 1. System preference base: use CSS variables */
@theme {
  --color-bg:         oklch(0.99 0 0);
  --color-surface:    oklch(0.96 0 0);
  --color-foreground: oklch(0.15 0 0);
  --color-muted:      oklch(0.55 0 0);
}

/* 2. Dark mode via .dark class on html element */
.dark {
  --color-bg:         oklch(0.12 0 0);
  --color-surface:    oklch(0.18 0 0);
  --color-foreground: oklch(0.95 0 0);
  --color-muted:      oklch(0.65 0 0);
}

/* 3. Respect OS preference when no explicit choice made */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:not(.light):not(.dark) {
    --color-bg:         oklch(0.12 0 0);
    --color-surface:    oklch(0.18 0 0);
    --color-foreground: oklch(0.95 0 0);
    --color-muted:      oklch(0.65 0 0);
  }
}

Three-state toggle implementation

type Theme = 'system' | 'light' | 'dark';

function applyTheme(theme: Theme) {
  const root = document.documentElement;
  root.classList.remove('light', 'dark');

  if (theme !== 'system') {
    root.classList.add(theme);
  }
  // 'system' = no class → CSS @media handles it

  localStorage.setItem('theme', theme);
}

// On page load — run before paint to prevent flash
const saved = localStorage.getItem('theme') as Theme ?? 'system';
applyTheme(saved);

Using semantic tokens in components

/* Components use semantic token names — never raw shades */

/* ❌ Wrong approach */
<div class="bg-white dark:bg-gray-900 text-gray-900 dark:text-white">

/* ✅ Correct approach — token resolves in the theme */
<div style="background: var(--color-bg); color: var(--color-foreground);">

/* Or via @theme-registered utilities: */
<div class="bg-bg text-foreground">
/* (if --color-bg is registered, bg-bg works automatically) */

Multi-theme system (light, dark, brand)

.theme-ocean {
  --color-bg:         oklch(0.97 0.02 220);
  --color-surface:    oklch(0.94 0.03 220);
  --color-foreground: oklch(0.20 0.05 220);
  --color-muted:      oklch(0.55 0.05 220);
  --color-primary:    oklch(0.50 0.15 240);
}

.theme-sunset {
  --color-primary: oklch(0.60 0.20 30);
}

Preventing flash of unstyled content (FOUC)

<!-- In HTML <head> — before any other script -->
<script>
  // Runs synchronously — no FOUC
  const t = localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'system';
  if (t === 'dark' || (t === 'system' && matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches)) {
    document.documentElement.classList.add('dark');
  }
</script>

Sable: "The FOUC script in the head is not optional for dark mode. Without it, users who prefer dark see a flash of white on every page load. That is a visible failure."

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Three states: system (follow OS), light (force light), dark (force dark). The OS preference is handled by @media. The user override is handled by adding .light or .dark to html. No class = follow OS. Two classes = chaos.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a dark-mode aware card using the semantic token pattern:

  • .theme-card: bg-white, dark:bg-gray-900, rounded-xl, border, border-gray-200, dark:border-gray-700, p-6, shadow-sm
  • .theme-title: text-gray-900, dark:text-white, text-lg, font-semibold, mb-2
  • .theme-body: text-gray-600, dark:text-gray-400, text-sm, leading-relaxed
  • .theme-badge: bg-blue-100, dark:bg-blue-900/40, text-blue-800, dark:text-blue-300, text-xs, font-medium, px-2, py-0.5, rounded-full
  • .theme-btn: w-full, mt-4, px-4, py-2, bg-blue-600, hover:bg-blue-700, dark:bg-blue-500, dark:hover:bg-blue-400, text-white, text-sm, font-medium, rounded-lg, transition-colors

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a complete three-state theme toggle component from scratch: system / light / dark buttons. Implement the applyTheme function that adds/removes .dark from html, stores the preference in localStorage, and handles the 'system' state. Include the FOUC-prevention script in a <script> tag. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three-state dark mode system (system / light / dark). What CSS mechanism handles the system preference? What JavaScript handles the user override? Why is the FOUC-prevention script in the HTML head essential, and what exactly does it prevent?

questions.prompt: In a professional three-state dark mode system, which mechanism handles the 'system' (OS preference) state when no user override is set?
options: @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) in CSS — applies dark variables when no .light or .dark class is on html
JavaScript matchMedia — runs on every page load to check OS preference
The dark: Tailwind variant — it automatically checks the OS preference
A service worker that injects the .dark class based on OS setting
questions.answer: @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) in CSS — applies dark variables when no .light or .dark class is on html
questions.explanation: The @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) query targets :root:not(.light):not(.dark) — it only applies when neither override class is present. The user's explicit .light or .dark class takes precedence over the OS preference. JavaScript is only needed for toggling the override.

questions.prompt: Why do dark mode users see a flash of white background on page load even when their theme preference is saved in localStorage?
options: Because the JavaScript that reads localStorage and applies .dark runs after the browser has already painted the initial white background
Because CSS transitions animate from white to dark on every load
Because localStorage is asynchronous and the theme resolves after paint
Because the dark: variant only activates after React mounts
questions.answer: Because the JavaScript that reads localStorage and applies .dark runs after the browser has already painted the initial white background
questions.explanation: The browser paints as soon as HTML+CSS is available — before deferred JavaScript runs. The fix is a synchronous <script> tag in the <head> (before the body renders) that reads localStorage and adds .dark to html immediately. This runs before any painting, preventing FOUC.

questions.prompt: A component uses bg-white dark:bg-gray-900 text-gray-900 dark:text-white across 50 files. Marketing wants a 'high contrast' theme as a third option. What is the problem with this approach, and what solves it?
options: Problem: adding a third theme requires adding new variant classes to all 50 files. Solution: semantic CSS variables (--color-bg, --color-foreground) that each theme overrides — components use bg-[var(--color-bg)] and never need updating
Problem: dark: classes only support two states. Solution: use @variant to define a high-contrast: variant
Problem: too many classes in the DOM. Solution: extract the classes into @apply rules
No problem — adding dark:bg-gray-950 classes for the third theme is manageable
questions.answer: Problem: adding a third theme requires adding new variant classes to all 50 files. Solution: semantic CSS variables (--color-bg, --color-foreground) that each theme overrides — components use bg-[var(--color-bg)] and never need updating
questions.explanation: Hardcoded dark: classes are a two-theme system by definition. Adding a third theme requires another variant across every component. Semantic CSS variables make theming a variable swap: define .theme-high-contrast { --color-bg: #000; --color-foreground: #fff; } and every component that uses var(--color-bg) automatically adapts.
